types.name: The Curious Fan
types.description: You notice what subtitles leave behind.

types.name: The Frustrated Learner
types.description: You know the rules, but real Korean keeps surprising you.

types.name: The Culture Explorer
types.description: You want language to make the culture feel closer.

types.name: The Low-Energy Learner
types.description: You want a tiny connection on days when studying feels like too much.

types.name: The Context Collector
types.description: You love saving little expressions and noticing patterns.

questions.text: You hear a Korean phrase in a drama. What do you do?

options.text: Screenshot it because I need to know what it really means.
Look up the grammar and try to make my own sentence.
Save it for later… then accidentally watch three more episodes.

questions.text: In a K-drama, someone calls a total stranger at a convenience store 언니 — not their actual sister. What's your reaction?

options.text: That's so interesting — it's not about family, it's about how Koreans build closeness through what they call each other.
Cute detail. I file it away and keep watching.
The subtitle just said 'excuse me' — that completely undersells what's happening.

questions.text: You notice a line ending in -다 instead of the -요 you're used to, and the subtitle reads exactly the same either way. What do you do?

options.text: Go down a grammar rabbit hole trying to nail down exactly when each one is 'correct.'
Jot both versions down side by side so I can compare them later.
Think about what kind of relationship or setting would make someone switch tone like that.

questions.text: A character says something like "이 정 때문에" and the subtitle just gives you "because I care about you." How do you feel about that?

options.text: Honestly, 'because I care' is close enough for me today.
That's exactly the kind of thing subtitles flatten — this word deserves its own explanation.
I want the precise definition, not a vibe — what does this word actually mean, technically?

questions.text: A variety show host repeats the same goofy catchphrase every single episode. What's your instinct?

options.text: I start a running list of catchphrases and which show or host each one is from.
I want to know the story behind it — why did this become the running joke?
I just laugh along and don't think about it any further — it's fun as-is.

questions.text: You come across an internet slang term that's genuinely common online but pretty harsh — the kind that comes with a "use with caution" note. What's your approach?

options.text: I want to understand exactly how and when it's used, even if it's an uncomfortable topic.
I want a clear line for when it's okay to just know it versus when it's okay to actually say it.
I file it under 'internet slang, handle carefully' for future reference.

questions.text: A drama shows a tense 회식 (mandatory-feeling company dinner) scene. What draws you into it?

options.text: The social dynamics — why does everyone act like attendance isn't optional when it clearly is?
Honestly I just want the vocabulary for ordering food and drinks — nothing deeper today.
The subtitle says 'company dinner,' but it completely misses the hierarchy tension in the room.

questions.text: Someone in a drama gets surprisingly serious about being addressed correctly as 선배. Why does that stick with you?

options.text: I want to know exactly who counts as 선배 versus 후배 in every setting — school, work, sports, all of it.
I add it to my growing list of relationship terms I'm collecting.
It shows how much respect and hierarchy is baked into just addressing someone by name.

questions.text: You spot an old-school internet slang ending in a chat, and it doesn't match anything from your textbook. What now?

options.text: I shrug, guess from context, and keep scrolling.
I stop everything to figure out exactly where this even came from.
I get a little frustrated that no textbook prepared me for this.

questions.text: After a week of K-dramas, you realize you've saved a dozen little expressions in your notes app and never reviewed a single one. How do you feel about that?

options.text: Thrilled — the collecting itself is half the fun.
I want to trace how they connect to bigger cultural patterns before I even think about reviewing.
No guilt — even glancing at the list later still counts as progress.
